research_concepts: split-half reliability of derived basketball metrics
year-over-year stability of team defensive traits
methodological_questions: How to isolate a defense's causal effect on opponent half-over-half change from other influences?
What is the appropriate reliability metric for a team's per-game H2-H1 opponent scoring difference?
What sample size (team-seasons, games) is needed to achieve adequate split-half and year-over-year reliability?
Does regression to the mean in opponent half-to-half scoring undermine the reliability estimate?
How to handle blowout games where garbage time may distort H2-H1 change?
Are there floor/ceiling effects (e.g., impossibility of large negative changes) that bias reliability estimates?

historical_evidence.finding: Split-half reliability of connector teammate-path quality Q_p (a player-level on-off PPP gap) is low: Pearson r=+0.215, Spearman-Brown ~0.355, ICC=0.216, most variance within-player half-to-half. Concluded not stable enough to treat as a scoutable trait.

Defensive scheme change within game and across games (inferred from opponent play-type PPP) shows high rates of apparent change (61% within-game, 68% cross-game) but near-uniform transition matrices consistent with label noise; cannot separate real defensive adjustment from offense executing differently.

Asymmetry, confidence, and carryover tests of A1 adapter PPP lift failed falsification: no-signal bucket outperformed adapters; effect did not widen with confidence; no carryover. Artifact attributed to selecting buckets on extreme early-third PPP, causing regression to the mean.

Usage-residual structural influence is a reproducible player property: pooled-residual split-half rank correlation ~0.67-0.69, partial ~0.56-0.56, showing that split-half reliability can be established for a well-specified, noise-filtered basketball metric.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Split-half reliability test of a player-level possession-derived quality metric.
failed_approaches.why: Low measurement reliability: within-player variance dominates, producing Spearman-Brown reliability far below the threshold for a stable trait.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferring defensive scheme change from opponent play-type performance outcomes.
failed_approaches.why: Label or classification error: near-uniform transition matrices indicate outcome-based labels cannot distinguish real defensive adjustments from offensive execution differences.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Testing asymmetric adapter responses, confidence gradients, and carryover using bucketed PPP deltas.
failed_approaches.why: Selection on extreme early-third PPP built in regression to the mean, producing spurious patterns and an artifact.

evidence_establishes: Split-half reliability of possession-derived basketball metrics can be low even with sample sizes of ~100 units, requiring careful noise filtering.
Inferring defensive characteristics directly from opponent performance outcomes risks label noise and regression-to-the-mean artifacts.
Well-specified metrics with appropriate controls can achieve high split-half reliability (FAM:SF18).
No prior study has directly tested the reliability of a team's opponent H2-H1 scoring change as a stable trait.
evidence_does_not_establish: The reliability of opponent H2-H1 change at the team level, aggregated over a full season and across seasons.
Whether the noise in half-over-half scoring differences is small enough relative to between-team signal to yield a reliable team trait.
The appropriate control variables and sample size needed to achieve adequate statistical power.
own_inferences: A defense's effect on opponent H2-H1 change can be conceptualized as a team-season average of game-level adjusted differentials (second half opponent points minus first half opponent points, or per-possession efficiency difference), after adjusting for opponent offensive strength, game location, and garbage time.

Team-level aggregation over 82 games per season should increase reliability beyond the player-season metrics that showed low reliability in FAM:SF-APPS-085, but the H2-H1 change is itself a noisy within-game measure.

The main confounders are: (a) opponent offensive quality, (b) game script and blowout-induced motivational changes, (c) regression to the mean from unusual first halves, (d) teammate and coach halftime adjustments not attributable to the defense's own systematic effect.

A properly designed test could use within-season split-half reliability (odd/even games) and year-over-year correlation as reliability benchmarks, with falsification tests including placebo shuffling of team identities and checking that reliability does not simply reflect opponent strength persistence.
uncertainties: Whether 120 team-seasons provide enough power to detect a moderate between-team variance component against within-team game-to-game noise.
The optimal way to handle garbage time (e.g., removing fourth quarters when spread exceeds a threshold) without introducing selection bias.
Whether a simple H2-H1 difference or a possession-adjusted efficiency difference is more stable and interpretable.
The degree to which year-over-year stability can be assessed given roster and coaching changes across seasons.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical evidence, a straightforward split-half and year-over-year reliability test might have been designed without sufficient safeguards. SF-APPS-085 shows that seemingly stable basketball measures can have low reliability; SF-APPA-001 demonstrates severe regression-to-the-mean artifacts when conditioning on performance extremes. These findings mandate that the design include (1) explicit control for first-half performance to mitigate regression to the mean, (2) comparison against null distributions via team-label permutation, and (3) a pilot within-season reliability check before committing to cross-season analyses. Thus the historical evidence caused the decision to change to proceed_with_changes with these additional design elements.

blocking_constraints.text: If the H2-H1 change is analysed conditional on extreme first-half performance, regression to the mean will inflate apparent stability or create spurious patterns.
The game-level H2-H1 opponent scoring difference has inherent noise; reliability may be too low to detect a team-level signal even with 82-game aggregation.
Opponent offensive strength, game script, and halftime adjustments by the opponent's coaching staff all contribute to H2-H1 change, making it difficult to isolate the defensive team's causal effect.

prior_work.summary: Prior work within this project has examined split-half reliability of player-level possession-derived metrics (SF-APPS-085, untestable due to low reliability) and defensive adaptation inferred from opponent outcomes (SF-APPA-005, untestable due to label noise; SF-APPA-001, artifact from regression to the mean). Another study (SF18) confirmed that well-filtered residual influence metrics can achieve high split-half reliability. No study has tested whether a defense's effect on opponent H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait. However, the existing evidence highlights risks that must be addressed: measurement reliability, regression to the mean, and confounded performance outcomes.

risks.text: Selecting or weighting games by extreme first-half opponent scoring would induce regression to the mean, artificially creating the appearance of a defensive effect or its reliability.
H2-H1 change per game is a noisy measure; even after aggregating to team-season level, the signal-to-noise ratio may be too low to achieve conventional reliability thresholds (e.g., ICC > 0.5).

Opponent offensive rating, roster quality, home/away status, and game context (e.g., blowouts, back-to-back games) influence H2-H1 change and must be controlled to avoid attributing these effects to the defense.

The H2-H1 change distribution is bounded by the impossibility of scoring negative points or extremely large swings, which can compress variance for strong defensive teams and bias reliability estimates.
Games with extreme blowouts or unusual circumstances (ejections, injuries) may need to be excluded, reducing effective sample size and power.
If multiple definitions of H2-H1 change (raw points, per-possession, adjusted models) are tested, multiplicity must be accounted for.

design.estimand: Team-season average of adjusted opponent H2-H1 scoring change (second-half opponent points minus first-half opponent points, per 100 possessions), representing the systematic effect of a team's defense on altering opponent scoring between halves, beyond what is expected from opponent offensive strength, venue, and first-half performance.
design.unit: Team-season (one team's full regular season, aggregated from ~82 game-level observations)
design.sample: 120 team-seasons from the NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons (30 teams × 4 seasons). Exclude playoff games for the primary analysis to avoid systematic differences in effort and strategy; a supplementary playoff-only analysis may be considered.
design.power: Assuming an intraclass correlation (ICC) of 0.20–0.40 based on prior basketball reliability work (SF-APPS-085), 120 team-seasons with 82 games each yields >80% power to detect an ICC of 0.25 in a two-level model (team vs. residual). For year-over-year correlation, 120 team-seasons (with repeat observations) can detect a Pearson correlation of 0.3 with approximately 80% power at alpha=0.05 two-sided. A simulation-based power analysis using the actual game-level noise variance from the data will confirm before confirmatory testing.
controls: Opponent offensive rating (points per 100 possessions) for the full season, entered as a linear covariate.
First-half opponent point total or per-possession efficiency to mitigate regression-to-the-mean bias.

Game-quarter indicator for garbage time: define a flag for games where the margin exceeds 20 points at halftime; primary analysis excludes these games; secondary analysis includes them with a control for fourth-quarter possessions when margin exceeds 20.
Rest days and back-to-back indicator for both the team and the opponent.
Season fixed effects to account for league-wide scoring trends.
falsification: Permutation test: randomly reassign team identities to each game within season and recompute the split-half reliability and year-over-year correlation; the true team label should yield ICC significantly above the permutation null distribution.

Placebo outcome: use opponent H1-H2 change (first half minus second half) – if a defense truly affects the H2-H1 change, the same team should not show a symmetrical effect in the opposite direction after controlling for first-half performance.
Check that the team's effect is not simply a function of its own offensive performance (e.g., slow pace leading to fewer opponent possessions in the second half).
design.multiplicity: Single primary metric: adjusted opponent H2-H1 scoring change per 100 possessions. Any exploratory analyses (raw points, per-half efficiency splits, etc.) will be declared secondary and not used for the decision. The decision rule uses a Bonferroni-corrected threshold if both within-season split-half and year-over-year correlation are tested as co-primary.
design.decision_rule: The trait is considered reliable if (a) within-season split-half Spearman-Brown reliability > 0.60 AND (b) year-over-year Pearson correlation of adjusted team-season averages > 0.30 with p < 0.025 (one-sided, adjusted for two tests). If either condition fails, the trait is deemed unreliable. If the permutation test shows the reliability is not significantly above chance, the study is invalidated.
design.data_version: Per-game files from the NBA stats API as available on 2026-10-06, with exact data cuts documented in a data commit hash. The primary analysis will use the 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons.

methodological_questions: What is the appropriate reliability measure for opponent adjustment metrics?
How to account for opponent offensive strength when computing H2-H1 change?
What is the impact of game script and blowout effects on H2-H1 differences?
How many games are needed for a stable team trait estimate?
Does regression to the mean affect H2-H1 change reliability?
Are there floor/ceiling effects in opponent scoring change?
args.query: Is a defense's effect on opponents' second-half minus first-half scoring change a reliable team-level trait, stable within and across seasons?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

reasoning_details.text: We need to identify research concepts and methodological questions from the task. The research question: "A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait." So it's about reliability of a measure. Concepts: defensive suppression, counter strategy, H2-H1 change (halftime score differential?), reliability? H2-H1 likely means second half minus first half point differential, maybe per game? It says "defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change". That could mean how much a defense causes opponents to score less in the second half compared to the first half, or change in scoring rate from first half to second half. This is a team trait: consistent across games, season, for a defense. So we need to test if this metric (opponent H2-H1 change when facing a particular defense) is stable (reliable) across time/contexts. The data has team-seasons. So we can compute for each team-season the average opponent H2-H1 change (maybe adjusted for opponent offense). Then test if this team-season metric correlates with itself across seasons, or split-half reliability within a season, etc. So research concepts: "defensive suppression", "halftime adjustment", "reliability", "team trait stability", "opponent scoring change", "second half vs first half". Methodological questions: reliability testing methods (intraclass correlation, split-half, test-retest), accounting for opponent quality, sample size, confounding by game script, regression to the mean, floor/ceiling effects, measurement error, etc. I'll craft a query summarizing the question. I'll retrieve history. Use tool retrieve_history. Pass research_concepts as list of strings, methodological_questions list, query string.

We need to produce the final output after stage 2. We have the retrieval result with 4 records: FAM:SF-APPS-085, FAM:SF-APPA-005, FAM:SF-APPA-001, FAM:SF18. We need to incorporate them into the output schema. But we might need more information: we can use follow-up tools within the budget of 12 calls (we already used 1, so 11 left). However, the instruction says: "Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned: 4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches. ... You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace." So we can still call tools to get more details, like read_family for the most relevant records to understand them fully. Let's decide which records are most relevant. The question is about reliability of defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change as a team trait. The records cover:

- FAM:SF-APPS-085: connector teammate-path quality Q_p split-half reliability. It's about split-half reliability of a player metric, not team defense H2-H1, but it's methodologically related (split-half reliability). It found untestable due to low reliability.

- FAM:SF-APPA-005: defensive scheme change within and across games (inferred labels). Found untestable due to label noise.

- FAM:SF-APPA-001: A1 adaptation falsification. Artifact, with risks of label error, mechanical floor.

- FAM:SF18: fragility confirmatory, split-half stability of residual influence, supported, but about a different construct (structural influence). However it uses split-half reliability successfully for that measure, showing some measures can be reliable.

But none directly addresses team defensive suppression of H2-H1 change. The most relevant might be the defensive scheme change study (FAM:SF-APPA-005) and the A1 adaptation study (FAM:SF-APPA-001), because they deal with halftime adjustments and defensive adaptation. However they are about scheme labels, not directly about H2-H1 scoring change reliability. The question is: "A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait." This is essentially a reliability/stability question. So the split-half reliability study of a different metric (FAM:SF-APPS-085) might give evidence about the difficulty of getting reliable metrics from play-by-play data, especially for opponent adjustments. The failure mechanism was low measurement reliability (split-half r=0.215). That suggests that trying to measure a team's defensive effect on H2-H1 change may face similar reliability problems. Also, the scheme change study suggests that inferred labels are noisy, which could affect measuring defensive adjustments. But H2-H1 change itself is not an inferred label; it's a directly observed scoring difference. However, isolating "a defense's effect" requires controlling for opponent offensive quality and game context. That still involves measurement challenges.

We might want to read the full family records for the most relevant ones to get details about their methods and limitations. We can call read_family for FAM:SF-APPS-085 (split-half reliability of connector metric) and maybe FAM:SF-APPA-005 and FAM:SF-APPA-001. But note the budget: 12 tools, we've used 1, we'll need to output final, but we can call read_family a few times and maybe explore_graph or data_catalog to understand what data fields are available. The data_catalog could tell us if we have per-game box scores, play-by-play, etc. The question mentions we have play-by-play, substitutions, defensive matchup minutes, box-score summary. So H2-H1 change can be computed per game for each opponent. We need to decide if we can measure a team's defensive trait reliably across games.

Let's call data_catalog() to see fields, then perhaps read_family for the relevant studies. But first, read the most directly relevant study that might have tried to measure defensive halftime adjustment reliability. Among the returned, none seems directly that. The A1 adaptation study (FAM:SF-APPA-001) might be about a similar concept: "A1 adapter PPP lift" might be about halftime adaptation of play types. It found artifact, due to label error and mechanical floor. That could be highly relevant. So read its full record.

Also FAM:SF-APPS-085's split-half reliability result may inform the likely reliability of any team-level split-half metric derived from play-by-play. So read that too.

I'll call read_family for FAM:SF-APPA-001 and FAM:SF-APPS-085, and also FAM:SF-APPA-005, maybe. Let's call them in parallel if possible, but we can only make one tool call per reply. So sequence: read_family FAM:SF-APPA-001, then read_family FAM:SF-APPS-085, then maybe explore_graph for some risks. But we need to stay within budget. We'll start with the most directly relevant: the A1 adaptation study (FAM:SF-APPA-001). Then the split-half reliability of connector metric. Then maybe FAM:SF-APPA-005 if still needed.

But we could also call explore_graph for risk nodes like MECHANICAL_FLOOR, LABEL_ERROR, MEASURE_RELIABILITY to see relationships. But we may get enough from read_family.
